# Antimicrobial-Resistance Screening {#sec-amr}

Every isolate PhyloTrace types is also screened for genes of clinical interest —
acquired antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) determinants, virulence factors, and
stress/biocide/metal-tolerance elements. This chapter explains what that screen
does, what it can and cannot tell you, and what it records. Visualizing the
results is @sec-amr-heatmap.

::: {.callout-tip title="Concept — genotype, not phenotype"}
A detected AMR gene means the isolate *carries a sequence known to contribute to
resistance*, not that it is measurably resistant in the laboratory. Screening
reports the **genotype**; clinical resistance also depends on whether the gene is
expressed, at what level, and in what combination with others. Treat a screening
result as a hypothesis to be confirmed by phenotypic testing, not as a
susceptibility report. See @sec-concepts-amr for more.
:::

## What the screen looks for {#sec-amr-scope}

The screen runs against NCBI's curated reference database and reports three
kinds of element together:

| Element type | What it means |
|---|---|
| **AMR** | An acquired resistance determinant, or a resistance-conferring point mutation |
| **VIRULENCE** | A gene contributing to pathogenicity |
| **STRESS** | Tolerance of biocides, metals or other stressors |

Keeping all three in one screen is deliberate: biocide and metal tolerance often
travel on the same mobile elements as resistance genes, so seeing them together
is informative when you are asking where a resistant lineage came from.

::: {.callout-important title="Point mutations are only called for supported species"}
Most findings are *acquired* genes — sequences the isolate has gained. Resistance
that arises instead from a **single base change in a core gene** can only be
called when the screening tool knows which organism it is looking at, and it
supports a fixed list of species.

PhyloTrace supplies the organism when your scheme's species is on that list, and
runs without it otherwise. In practice: acquired genes, virulence and stress
elements are **always** detected; point mutations are detected **only when the
species is supported**. If you are working on an unsupported species, absence of
point-mutation findings tells you nothing.
:::

## When it runs {#sec-amr-when}

The screen is step 3 of the typing run (@sec-typing-pipeline) — it happens
automatically for each assembly, right after that assembly has been typed. There
is no separate "run AMR" action.

If the screen fails or exceeds its time limit for a particular isolate, that is
recorded and the run moves on; the isolate's allele profile and sequence type are
unaffected. Re-typing an isolate replaces its previous AMR findings rather than
adding to them, so an isolate never accumulates duplicate calls.

## What is recorded {#sec-amr-results}

PhyloTrace keeps two complementary views of the result for each isolate.

**The detailed view** — one entry per detected element, carrying:

- the gene symbol and the reference sequence it matched,
- the element type (AMR / virulence / stress),
- the drug class and subclass the element is associated with,
- how good the match was (percent identity and percent coverage),
- where in the assembly it was found.

**The curated summary** — a per-isolate roll-up by drug class, which is what the
drug-class heatmap draws (@sec-amr-heatmap). It distinguishes three categories:

| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Match** | A confident call for that drug class |
| **Partial** | An incomplete or lower-confidence hit |
| **Virulence** | A virulence determinant rather than a resistance one |

::: {.callout-important title="A partial call is never shown as a confident one"}
The match/partial distinction is preserved everywhere the results are displayed,
and where both would land in the same cell the more confident one is shown.
Reading a partial as confident would overstate an isolate's resistance, so the
distinction is worth attending to when you read a heatmap.
:::

## Traceability {#sec-amr-provenance}

The outcome of the screen, the organism it was run with, whether point mutations
were called, how many elements were found, and the versions of the screening
tools and their reference database are all recorded on the isolate's provenance
record (@sec-typing-provenance).

::: {.callout-important title="Why the reference-database version matters"}
AMR reference databases are updated frequently. An isolate screened last year and
one screened today may legitimately differ in their findings without either being
wrong. Before comparing AMR results across a collection built over time, check
that they were screened against the same database version — the provenance record
is where that is written down.
:::

## Chapter summary

- Screening runs automatically with typing and reports acquired AMR genes,
  virulence factors and stress elements together.
- Point mutations require a supported species; everything else is always
  detected.
- A failed screen never costs you the allele profile; re-typing replaces previous
  findings rather than duplicating them.
- Results are kept both in detail (one entry per element) and as a curated
  drug-class summary that distinguishes confident from partial calls.
- Tool and reference-database versions are recorded per isolate, which is what
  makes AMR results comparable over time.

@sec-amr-heatmap turns these results into presence/absence and drug-class views.
